title: Mental Stealth: Student Life and Self-Care
content_markdown:
January always arrives with a lot of expectations\. New calendars, new deadlines, new energy we’re all supposed to magically have after the break; even though it’s cold, dark, and my brain is still very much in winter mode\. 

As a student, January doesn’t always feel like a fresh start\. It feels like pressure\. 

Midterms start creeping up almost immediately\. Papers pile on\. Group projects reappear\. And somehow, in between all of that, I’m expected to keep my life together? Show up to work, keep up with extracurriculars, eat real meals, and maintain a social life\. Most days, I manage\. From the outside, it probably looks like I’m doing fine\. 

And that’s kind of the problem\. 

## The Quiet Way Mental Health Shows Up

Physical health tends to be loud\. When I’m sick, my body makes it obvious — I feel run down, exhausted, and eventually forced to slow down\. 

Mental health is quieter\. It doesn’t always announce itself the way physical illness does\. 

What I’ve noticed, especially in university, is how easy it is to keep functioning even when something feels off\. Classes still get attended, assignments still get submitted, and messages still get answered with a casual “I’m busy\.” 

I think of this as ‘*mental stealth’–st*ruggling internally while still appearing put\-together and capable\. It’s not always dramatic, and it’s not always immediately noticeable — *even* to ourselves\. 

And the more I’ve learned about mental health, the more I’ve realized how common this experience is\. Nearly **half of people who struggle with depression or anxiety have never sought professional help**, meaning many people carry these experiences quietly\. In British Columbia, **1 in 5 people will experience a mental health issue at some point in their lives**, which puts this quiet kind of struggle into perspective\. 

## When Being Overwhelmed Feels Normal

One of the most challenging aspects of student life is how normalized stress has become\. Being exhausted is expected\. Being overwhelmed is relatable\. Running on caffeine and deadlines feels like part of the culture\. 

I’ve caught myself minimizing my own feelings because everyone else seems just as busy, just as tired\. I tell myself this is just what university is like\. I’ll deal with it later: after this midterm, after this paper, after reading break\. Later keeps moving\.

Mental stealth thrives in that mindset\. When struggle is common, it becomes harder to recognize when it’s actually taking a toll\. You don’t need to be at a breaking point to deserve support\. 

## Acknowledging Mental Health and Finding Support

One thing I’ve come to realize is that needing support doesn’t mean something has gone wrong, it just means something needs attention\. Mental health struggles don’t always show up as crises, and they don’t have to reach a breaking point to be valid\. Sometimes it’s simply noticing that things feel heavier than usual, or that getting through the day takes more effort than it used to\. 

Because these experiences are so common, support exists for such moments too\. Organizations like the **Canadian Mental Health Association** share accessible information, and at UBC there are resources such as **Counselling Services**, **Student Health Services**\. Knowing these options exist has been a reminder that struggling silently isn’t a personal failure, and that support can be part of everyday care, not just emergencies\. 

Mental stealth might make it easier to keep going, but it doesn’t have to mean doing everything alone\. Taking mental health seriously, even in subtle, quiet ways, is still an important step toward feeling better\.

*This blogpost was based on [a previous resource](https://learningcommons.ubc.ca/mental-stealth-student-life-and-self-care/) published on January 2016\.*

title: I Tried It! Waking Up at 5 AM for a Week
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/04/julian-hochgesang-Wd8gStxy3s-unsplash-1-940x627.jpg)

Image by Julian Hochgesang on Unsplash

Does waking up at 5 AM actually change your life, or is it just Instagram hype? We’ve all seen those reels and read those self\-help books that swear by it, the secret of billionaires, athletes, and traditionally “successful” people\. I’ll admit, I got curious\. So, I decided to try it myself: waking up at 5 AM for a week and seeing if it really lives up to the hype\.

## Day 1: The Messy Start

Let’s be real, my first day was rough\. I went to bed at midnight \(rookie mistake\) and got maybe 5 hours of sleep\. Technically, I did wake up at 5… but all that meant was opening my eyes, scrolling on my phone in bed, and maybe sneaking in a nap around 7\. By 8:30, I realised this wasn’t the kind of “transformative” morning I had in mind\.

## Day 2: Learning that Routine Starts at Night

That day I did some research and learned something important: a 5 AM morning starts the night before\. Our bodies need at least 7 hours of sleep \(if not more\), otherwise the early wake\-up just backfires\. So I made myself go to sleep by 10 PM\. I also made a simple morning plan so I wouldn’t just end up doom\-scrolling again\. 

The next morning felt different\. Sure, I was still groggy, but I got up, meditated, did some yoga, and actually made a proper breakfast\. That slow start meant I wasn’t rushing through my day, I felt more prepared, calmer, and surprisingly organized\. \(Yes, I was still yawning a lot, but at least I wasn’t sprinting from one task to another\.\) 

## Day 3: Structure, Wins and…Slips

By Day 3, I added time stamps to my routine\. Having a mini\-schedule helped me get so much done before 9 AM\. I studied, worked on extracurriculars, even sent emails that I’d been procrastinating to my professors\. Plus, I ate more than just a banana for breakfast\.   

Then came Day 4\. Let’s just say a friend’s birthday dinner \+ me pretending I can survive on less than 5 hours of sleep \= the alarm had no chance\. I woke up at 9, and honestly? The cake was worth it\.

## Day 5\-7: Motivation, Mindfulness, and Finding Balance

Getting back into routine on Day 5 was tough\. I had to remind myself why I was doing this: those peaceful, slow mornings where I didn’t feel rushed\. That thought kept me going\. For the last couple of days, I mixed in some mindfulness activities\. One morning, I tried a puzzle \(spoiler: it stressed me out more than it calmed me\), and the next I did some painting, which I’d *highly* recommend\. It was surprisingly grounding and definitely took the edge off midterm stress\.

## So, would I do it again?

Honestly? As a university student, 5 AM feels a little extreme\. Between late\-night assignments, 11:59 PM deadlines, and just hanging out with friends, it’s not always realistic\. But here’s what I *did* learn: slow, intentional mornings are worth it\.

I’ve decided I’ll start waking up around 7 instead of 9\. Those extra two hours still give me the space to breathe, eat, plan, and not feel like I’m chasing the day\. And that, in itself, feels like a win\. 

Maybe I’m not cut out for the 5 AM club just yet, but I’ve found my own version that works, and I think that’s the point\. Everyone’s “ideal” looks a little different\. So, comment down below, what’s yours? What’s the wake\-up time that makes you feel your best?

title: Vancouver Summer Bucket List
content_markdown:
After months of near\-constant cloud coverage and nonstop rain, the sun finally starts to show its bright, beautiful face around May and Vancouver becomes so fun and vibrant\. I have compiled a list of my favourite summer activities\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/04/image-1-940x348.png)

# Centennial Seawalk

### West Vancouver

[*Image from 10adventures\.com*](https://www.10adventures.com/hikes/north-shore/centennial-seawalk/)

This scenic walk is a must\-visit in Vancouver\. It’s a 1\.7 km walk from Ambleside beach to Dundrave beach\. The walk provides stunning views of Burrard Inlet, the mountains, and the city of Vancouver\. It’s the perfect place to go if you love the Stanley Park Seawall but want to try out a less\-busy spot\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/04/image-2-940x628.png)

# The Khatsahlano Street Party

### Kitsilano, Vancouver

*[Image by Jon Benjamin Photography\.](https://www.createastir.ca/articles/khatsahlano-street-party-2023)*

The Khatsahlano Street Party is one of the most fun events of the summer\. It spans 10 blocks and features amazing live music, cool vendors, and delicious food trucks\. It’s one of my favourite free summer festivals and is definitely worth checking out\. This summer, it’s happening Saturday, July 11th from 11:00 am to 9:00 pm\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/04/VAG_exterior_2023_03.jpg)

# By Donation Day

### Vancouver Art Gallery

*[Image by Ian Lefebvre\.](https://historicplacesdays.ca/places/vancouver-art-gallery/)*

Situated in the heart of Downtown Vancouver is the historic Vancouver Art Gallery\. The Gallery hosts amazing exhibitions and houses incredible artworks from the likes of Emily Carr to Pablo Picasso\. It’s a classic museum in the city because they have a good mix of traditional and modern art\. The first Friday of every month from 4 pm – 8 pm, admission is by donation\. Make sure to book in advance because spots fill up fast\!

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/04/Shipyards-Night-Market-1400x933-1.jpg)

# Shipyards Night Market

### North Vancouver

[*Image from vancouversnorthshore\.ca\.*](https://www.vancouversnorthshore.com/signatureevent/shipyardsnightmarket/)

A great way to spend a hot summer  evening is at Shipyards Nightmarket in North Vancouver\. It’s a free market that happens every Friday, 3:00 pm to 10:00 pm, from May to September\. Local vendors and food trucks set up shop all down the waterfront\. It’s a perfect, fun summer evening\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/04/429d08cdf37146c6095ff03568c4172642ca443d-7547x5031-1.webp)

# Lynn Canyon

### North Vancouver

*[Image from destinationvancouver\.com\.](https://www.destinationvancouver.com/things-to-do/listings/lynn-canyon-suspension-bridge)*

Lynn Canyon is the perfect place for a fun summer adventure because it’s a chill hike with beautiful scenery, a suspension bridge, waterfalls, and a natural swimming pool\. It’s the perfect place to cool off on a hot summer day by walking in the shade or taking a dip in the natural pool\. Lynn Canyon is dog\-friendly and accessible by public transit and car\!

---

These are just a few of my favourite summer activities, but Vancouver truly comes to life in the summer, so there are many other activities happening all over the city\! Make sure to go out this summer and check them out\!

title: Unions 101: A (Near) Graduate’s Guide to Figuring Out Collective Action for Workers
content_markdown:
*This blog is written the purpose of raising awareness about the basic functions, how they work, and why they’re important for students to learn about\!* 

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/05/Photo-by-The-New-York-Public-Library-on-Unsplash.jpg)

As I approach the end of my undergraduate degree and grow ever closer to entering the workforce \(or the intimidating academia field\), there’s been a few things that I’ve realised are important\. In my preoccupation with stressful deadlines, part\-time jobs, and trying to get my foot in the ‘working adult’ door, I never really paid attention to serious issues that could affect me down the line – like equitable benefits and fair wages\. As I finish my degree though, it’s growing clearer that good working conditions are essential to making sure young professionals aren’t taken advantage of\. With that in mind, here’s a few things you may not know \(I certainly didn’t\) about unions\.

*[Image](https://unsplash.com/photos/grayscale-photo-of-men-Ml4gbZAk4RE?asset=%5B%22Photos%22%2C%7B%22slug%22%3A%22grayscale-photo-of-people-standing-near-buildings-9Rk7goDMzvw%22%7D%5D): Works Progress Administration \(WPA\) workers protesting congressional cut of relief appropriations\. \(1939\)\. Dorothea Lange\.*

## First, what is a union? 

A union is composed of a group of workers who join to negotiate better working conditions with employers\. Let me put it this way – it’s a bunch of people trying to make sure working professionals aren’t taken advantage of\. This includes advocating for different kinds of benefits like fairer and higher wages\! 

## How do unions work? 

Unions are formed when a worker majority in a workspace vote for a representing party, or when an employer voluntarily recognises a group of worker representatives as a union\. The group must then be recognised by a board, after which they become official\! After all of this, employers and union members come together to create a [Collective Bargaining Agreement](https://www.lrb.bc.ca/collective-bargaining) \(CBA\) that is used by both parties to negotiate provisions like health insurance benefits, wages, and vacation time\. 

## Unions at UBC\! 

Undergraduates figuring out what to do with their degrees are exposed to so many opportunities it can be overwhelming\. At UBC, research assistant positions and part\-time work are incredibly inviting opportunities\. However, my experiences working part\-time around Vancouver and at UBC have taught me that it’s important to know where we stand as young professionals – if only, so that the ideas and innovation we bring with us are compensated fairly\. 

Now, I’ve learnt that at UBC, there’s a considerable union presence\. The [UBC Faculty Association](https://www.facultyassociation.ubc.ca/) is the biggest amongst these and is committed to creating academic freedom and equity at the institution\. Nowadays, there are even more voices determined to be heard\. For instance, graduate students working as Research Assistants at UBC have expressed their commitment towards unionising as well\. Over [3000](https://www.cupe.bc.ca/2023/05/15/ubc-research-assistants-to-join-cupe-in-the-largest-successful-union-organizing-campaign-in-recent-b-c-history/) graduate researchers have [petitioned](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/ubc-research-assistant-certification-1.6845948) to join the [Canadian Union of Public Employees](https://cupe.ca/) \(CUPE\), British Columbia’s largest union\! 

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/05/UBC-Brand-and-Marketing-edited-scaled.jpg)

*UBC Brand & Marketing\.*

## So, why are unions important? 

There’s a couple of reasons why I think unions are such an integral part of creating an equitable work environment\. The most important reason I could think of is fairly obvious – avoiding exploitation\. I believe that even undergraduate students contribute to work and research spaces in 

a way that impacts how institutions function\. So even if you don’t plan on joining a union at this very moment, I do think it’s important to know at least the basics of how they work, since I believe they’re an essential part of today’s professional world\!

title: My Favourite Cozy Games for a Night In
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/05/bryan-natanael-kYfVYyT4kEg-unsplash.jpg)

As the cold seeps into Vancouver’s streets and the rain starts its daily performance, it’s officially the season of fuzzy socks, hot drinks, and indoor game nights that last way too long\. Whether you’re hosting a cozy night in or procrastinating on that one assignment \(we’ve all been there\), here are some of my favourite games to play with friends when it’s too chilly to step outside\. 

## **Charades**

Yes, it’s a classic, but the *movie edition*? Instead of acting out random words, you only act out *movie titles*, and the more dramatic, bizarre, or obscure they are, the funnier it gets\. My go\-tos? “Come Forth and Bear Witness to My Unscrupulous Wang,” and “A Lizard in a Woman’s Skin\.” Watching your friends act these out is priceless, and the confused faces trying to guess? Even better\. Bonus: you might just discover your next movie\-night pick\.

## **Guess Who: Personal Edition**

Okay, I’m claiming this one, I *think* I invented it \(please don’t ruin my dream 😅\)\. The rules? Simple\. One person secretly picks someone you all know: could be your first RA, a random cafe barista, or that one friend\-of\-a\-friend everyone met once\. Then everyone fires off yes\-or\-no questions until someone cracks the case\. It sounds harmless… until you’re three rounds deep arguing over who counts as “mutual\.”

## **Cards**

### 1\. Playing Cards

You can *never* go wrong with classic old cards\. I once played Bluff until 6 AM \(partly because I was winning, but who’s counting? …clearly not me\)\. Whether it’s Bluff, Spoons, or just an excuse to sip hot chocolate under a blanket, it’s the perfect weekend ritual\. You can find rules for these games and many more such games on this [website](https://bicyclecards.com/how-to-play)\! 

### 2\. Uno

The game that destroys friendships and builds character\. Everyone has “their” UNO rules \(and apparently none of them match\)\. Between “UNO: No Mercy” and everyone pretending *their* house rules are the real ones, it’s the one game where my competitive side instantly comes alive\.

### 3\. Monodeal

Fifteen minutes of chaos and strategy\. One card can flip the entire game\. You’ll be a real estate mogul one second and completely broke the next… unless, of course, you’ve got a “Just Say No\.” If you know, you *know\.* If you don’t, it’s time to find out\.

Games like these are exactly why indoor nights hit different\. One minute I’m convinced I’ve mastered the rules, the next I’m begging my friends for mercy and wondering how the game turned on me so fast\. It’s that mix of competitiveness, ridiculousness, and the kind of laughter that warms me from the inside out\. Add blankets, warm drinks, fuzzy socks, and the rain humming in the background, and suddenly the whole night feels soft, cozy, and exactly where I truly want to be\.

So here’s to warm rooms, late\-night giggles, and inside jokes born from pure game\-night madness\. If you try any of these out, tell us which one had you laughing the hardest or share your go\-to game that always steals the show in the comments below\!

title: CLCA Favourites: Electives Worth Your Time
content_markdown:
Choosing courses can be tricky\. I know what it’s like to want electives that won’t tank your GPA\. However, the best classes are often the ones that challenge us, make us curious, and leave us thinking long after the final exam\. I believe a good course doesn’t have to be easy; it just has to make you curious and keep you engaged\.

The Chapman Learning Commons Peer Advisors have put together a list of courses that stood out, not because they were simple, but because we actually enjoyed taking them\. Whether you’re looking to explore new ideas, build practical skills, or just see things from a fresh perspective, these courses offer something unique worth checking out\.

*Image by [Beatriz Camaleo](https://unsplash.com/illustrations/a-stack-of-books-with-an-apple-on-top-1Pkjk2pAYR4) on Unsplash*

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/05/Picture1.png)

## **ASIA 308** – **Myths of India**

An intriguing journey through Vedic and Indo\-European mythologies\. Our CLCA explored epics like the Mahabharata and saw how these stories reflect spiritual and cultural shifts\. The course offers a laid\-back but meaningful look at the myths that shaped South Asian thought and religion\.

**Why we love it:** A chance to dive into epic stories while exploring how myths shaped entire cultures\.

## **ASTR 310 – Survey of the Solar System**

A must\-take if you’ve ever stared up at the night sky in awe\. This course explores recent planetary discoveries, the Sun, and the search for life, no advanced math required\.

**Why we love it:** A science course that’s fascinating, accessible, and literally out of this world\.

## **ARCL 235 – Taming the Wild: Animals, Alcohol, and Agriculture**

A fascinating course about how humans domesticated plants and animals over thousands of years\. Expect some challenging memorization, but the rich content from early agriculture to brewing keeps it engaging\.

**Why we love it:**  You’ll never look at farming, food, or fermentation the same way again\.

## **APSC 367 / POLI 371 – Humanitarian Engineering: Politics and Practice**

A collaborative experience uniting engineering, political science, and IR students\. Teams work with NGOs on real\-world problems, like water purification for underserved communities\.

**Why we love it:** Hands\-on, impactful learning that connects engineering to global change\.

## **CPSC 103 – Introduction to Systematic Program Design**

A friendly introduction to coding for complete beginners\. Students gain core computational and logical thinking skills without the intimidation\.

**Why we love it:** Makes coding approachable and surprisingly even enjoyable for people who never thought they’d code\.

## **CRWR 200 – Introduction to Creative Writing**

A joyful, confidence\-building course that celebrates creativity in every form, from poetry to screenplays to children’s fiction\. Professor Taylor Evans’s fun teaching style and interactive slides make each class a highlight of the week\. Manuscript submission is not required for admission\.

**Why we love it:** Known as both a GPA and an inspiration booster; wildly fun and freeing\.

## **CRWR 203 – Writing for Children**

An engaging and hands\-on introduction to children’s literature\. The instructor encourages creativity through interactive assignments and discussions on character\-building, pacing, and storytelling across age groups\.

**Why we love it:** Imaginative, playful, and perfect if you want a creative outlet\.

## **FRST 303 – Into the Woods: An Introduction to Forest Science**

An unexpectedly refreshing course for students curious about nature\. It covers topics such as tree biology, forest ecology, and environmental issues, including wildfires and fungi\.

**Why we love it:** Blends science with creativity; the tree\-tracking assignment makes you see nature in a totally new, personal way\.

## **NURS 180 – Stress and Resilience**

A refreshing change of pace from heavy academic loads, this course focuses on resilience, stress, and self\-care\. It offers practical strategies for maintaining mental, emotional, and physical well\-being, perfect for anyone looking to navigate student life more calmly and confidently\.

**Why we love it:** Teaches real\-life self\-care skills every student wishes they had learned sooner\.

## **PHIL 220 – Symbolic Logic**

This course covers sentential and predicate logic, including techniques for translating natural language statements into formal logical expressions\. It also explores truth tables and systems of natural deduction\.

**Why we love it:** Sharpens your thinking and gives you reasoning superpowers you’ll use everywhere\.

## **POLI 378 – The Politics of Terrorism**

A really eye\-opening look at terrorism as both a political strategy and a social idea\. The readings and discussions delve into the motives, origins, and various ways people attempt to counter it, making the whole topic feel much more layered and understandable\.

**Why we love it:** Intellectually gripping and taught in a way that keeps every class lively\.

---

The right course can surprise you, challenge you, and even make you excited to show up on a Monday morning\. From exploring the solar system to crafting children’s stories, these electives prove that learning can be fun, memorable, and meaningful\. Whether you’re looking to boost your creativity, sharpen your reasoning, or dive into something completely new, these CLCA\-recommended courses are great places to start\.

Have you tried any of them? Do you have a course that deserves a shout\-out? Drop your recommendations below\.

title: Tips for Camping for the First Time
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/05/dave-hoefler-a3e7yEtQxJs-unsplash.jpg)

*Photo by [Dave Hoefler](https://unsplash.com/@iamthedave) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/a-tent-set-up-in-the-woods-at-sunset-a3e7yEtQxJs)*

Camping is one of my favourite ways to unplug from the stress of school, allowing me to relax and reconnect with nature\. When I first got into camping, however, I was definitely a little nervous\. I had no clue what to pack, how to set up a tent, or what to expect from sleeping outside\. Now, after my first few camping trips, I’ve learned a few things that made the experience way less stressful and way more fun\. Here are a few things I would recommend for any first\-time campers:

## **Tip 1: Keep Gear Simple**

I used to think I needed every gadget in the outdoor section of the store\. The reality? A basic tent, sleeping bag, and flashlight were all I really needed\. My favourite brands of [tents](https://www.colemancanada.ca/tents-shelters/tents-by-style/), [sleeping bags](https://www.mountainwarehouse.com/ca/camping/sleeping-bags/?_gl=1*15ovlhu*_up*MQ..*_gs*MQ..*_ga*MTk0ODkwNDAwNS4xNzU4NzgxMTg2*_ga_3F0STYNNTV*czE3NTg3ODExODYkbzEkZzEkdDE3NTg3ODExODYkajYwJGwwJGg5MDQzMTU5NA..&gclid=Cj0KCQjwrc7GBhCfARIsAHGcW5U9H5HTmBhnq0brctWTLaKlrcZJ6YlxCL0y4GvcEove-EDSjZkIt_YaAtuIEALw_wcB&gbraid=0AAAAADoKbU_TAn_m70lsslXBb2h9CUl51), and [flashlights](https://nitecorestore.com/collections/flashlights) have consistently held up year after year, making camping a whole lot easier\. Keeping things simple made packing easier, allowing me to focus on enjoying nature instead of worrying about losing or damaging my belongings\.

## **Tip 2: Practice Setting Up Tents**

My first trip involved a lot of trial and error as I attempted to set up my tent, wasting valuable hiking time on trying to figure out where the poles and stakes went\. Now, I set up my tent in my

backyard or living room at least once before going out to refresh my memory\. It saves a lot of stress at the campsite, and I feel way more confident when I arrive\.

## **Tip 3: Pack Smart Snacks**

I’ve learned that bringing food that’s easy to carry and won’t spoil helps a lot during the camping trip\. I like to pack trail mix, granola bars, and beef jerky for quick snacks during hikes\. I also like to bring ingredients for simple campfire meals, like hot dogs, or a mix of marshmallows, chocolate, and graham crackers \(for s’mores, of course\!\)\. Cooking over the campfire can take a bit of practice, so I recommend watching some [tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JD6_VqAcfA) beforehand to prepare\. I’ve found that having both snacks and easy\-to\-cook meals keeps me fuelled and makes the whole experience way more fun\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/05/leon-contreras-5mB9Hndmsfk-unsplash.jpg)

*Photo by [Leon Contreras](https://unsplash.com/@lc_photography) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/person-barbecuing-marshmallow-5mB9Hndmsfk)*

## **Tip 4: Bring Extra Layers**

On my first ever camping trip, I remember waking up in the middle of the night shivering\. Now, I always bring extra layers, even if it’s warm during the day\. A light fleece jacket makes a huge difference for colder nights, while not adding much weight or bulk to my bag\.

## **Tip 5: Make a Checklist for the Small Things**

In the rush of packing and heading to the campsite, I always seem to forget something, like toilet paper, a first\-aid kit, or a phone charger\. Those little things are easy to miss but always crucial\. Now, I make a quick checklist before every trip\. It helps me feel prepared without overpacking\.

---

Camping for the first time can feel overwhelming, but these simple tips have made my trips way more enjoyable\. Even when things don’t go perfectly, try and remember that it’s all about enjoying the outdoors, and slowing down from the busyness of life\.

title: I Tried It! Shinrin-yoku, aka Forest Bathing
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/steven-kamenar-MMJx78V7xS8-unsplash-scaled-1.jpg)

Photo by [Steven Kamenar](https://unsplash.com/@skamenar?utm_content=creditCopyText&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=unsplash) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/photography-of-tall-trees-at-daytime-MMJx78V7xS8?utm_content=creditCopyText&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=unsplash)

Whenever I’m feeling stressed or overwhelmed, my instinct is to retreat home and recharge\. But staying indoors too long can backfire, especially when I end up scrolling on my phone instead of actually unwinding\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/unnamed-1.jpg)

Dr\. Sally Aitken’s “Into the Woods” course \(designed for forest science newbies like me\) introduced me to the Japanese practice of *shinrin\-yoku*, or forest bathing, which entails visiting a forest and immersing yourself in the experience\. [Cleveland Clinic \(2023\)](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/why-forest-therapy-can-be-good-for-your-body-and-mind) notes that, although research on forest bathing is still relatively new, studies suggest that it can benefit our overall wellbeing, both physically and mentally\. What drew my attention most is its potential to reduce stress, anxiety, and depression

Given how stressed I’ve been while juggling school, work, and life, I decided to give forest bathing a try for the month of October\. *After all*, I thought, *my commute takes me by Pacific Spirit Regional Park—why not go someday after class?* I’ve also been wanting to connect with nature, and this seemed like a great alternative to hiking or camping, which I’ve never been athletic or outdoorsy enough to enjoy\.

On my first outing, my sister, dog, and I followed a quiet trail when a loud hammering noise caught our attention\. Trusting my amateur birding instincts, I peeked around a tree and came face\-to\-face with a pileated woodpecker\! I was thrilled, the woodpecker was unfazed, and my sister took a video \(screenshot included\)\.

Since then, I’ve been to Pacific Spirit Park once more\. Both experiences were a breath of fresh air, but I felt most at peace when I went by myself, likely because I was better able to focus on my surroundings\. While I’m unable to \(dis\)prove any claims about the effects of forest bathing based on this very brief, personal experiment, I *have* noticed that mindful walks in the woods help steady my breathing, relax my facial muscles, and clear my head\.

But I’ll be honest, it’s hard to muster the energy or find time to visit the forest frequently\. While “park bathing” may not be as effective as forest bathing, something is better than nothing, so I’ve taken advantage of more accessible ways to explore the outdoors\. 

The adjacent image shows the golden canopy of a horsechestnut tree in my neighbourhood\. Moments before a rogue chestnut nearly concussed me, I was appreciating how the leaves rustled gently in the breeze and how the sunlight filtered through them… It feels cheesy writing this, but I swear, the clichés are clichés for a reason\! Paying attention to things like this helps me ground myself in the present and take a break from deadlines and everyday worries\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/unnamed-2-scaled-1.jpg)

If you want to explore nature while also practicing a little mindfulness, consider giving forest \(or perhaps park\) bathing a try\. There are many green spaces on or near campus that are worth exploring\. I particularly enjoy visiting Nitobe Memorial Garden, Pacific Spirit Park, and Jericho Beach Park\. Based on my experience, even a brief time outdoors can help soothe stress and provide perspective\. Who would’ve thought touching grass is actually good for us?

Let us know if you try forest bathing and how it makes you feel\! If you’d like a guide to some common plants and critters to look for on your walks, check out Jaya’s blogpost [here](https://learningcommons.ubc.ca/common-plants-and-animals-found-on-campus/)\.

**Reference**

title: Style: Discovering Yourself
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/Picture1.png)

Stock photo 1 by [ethanbodnar](https://unsplash.com/@ethanbodnar) on [Unsplash](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1534639077088-d702bcf685e7?q=80&w=1065&auto=format&fit=crop&ixlib=rb-4.1.0&ixid=M3wxMjA3fDB8MHxwaG90by1wYWdlfHx8fGVufDB8fHx8fA%3D%3D), 2 on [pixabay](https://pixabay.com/photos/blue-jeans-belt-belt-buckle-buckle-2160265/) , 3 by CLCA Selene Nguyen, and 4 on [pixabay](https://pixabay.com/photos/sewing-thimble-pins-safety-pins-661992/)

## 1\. Style is not what they think\.

Fashion journalist Lynn Yaeger was once asked in an interview what the best advice she had ever received was\. She replied, *“Oh, it’s from Sally Singer: if you are interested in fashion, you need to learn everything except fashion” \(@voguemagazine \(2023\)* At first, the advice struck me as completely counterintuitive\. But the more I thought about it, the more it made sense\. I think perhaps putting a reference in would be good, either as a footnote or mentioning the publication? We might have to do it for copyright\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/Picture2.png)

Looking back, I can see the advice played out during my time at our university\. It is easy to lose your sense of individuality where everyone is trying to be the better version of themselves, especially with a competitive environment like UBC\. Additionally, social media constantly tells us what is *right* to wear, making cultivating a truly individual style feel almost impossible\.

## 2\. Style is what you define it as\.

The reason *style* can feel overwhelming is because most students often confuse being *fashionable* with *having style\.* As a computer science student, style to me simply means pulling on comfortable sweatpants so I can power through a programming assignment; other times, it’s a professional blouse that reflects my aspiration to make it in our world\. No doubt – at times my style can feel performative of who I am\. However, I am the director of my image even in those moments\.

What makes style essential is that it signals intention: this is who I want the world to witness\.

## 3\. Style is more than just garments\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/Picture3.png)

Stock photo on [Pixabay](https://pixabay.com/illustrations/painting-classical-oil-painting-8598152/)

I hope by now I’ve planted enough reasons for you to see why a sense of style matters\. But now you might ask, how do I actually style myself? Let’s return to that counterintuitive advice: it’s everything but fashion\. Start by mapping what resonates with you on an individual level\. These are the building blocks to construct your own style\. For example, most of my inspirations are drawn from the events I have attended on campus\. One of the more memorable pieces was capturing the patterns of the lion dance costumes at queer lunar new year that I organized for AMS\!

## 4\. Style is classics and rebels\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/Picture4.png)

Stock photo on [Pixabay](https://pixabay.com/photos/piano-musical-instrument-1522856/)

Once you have a foundation to build your style on, one trick that always helps me during a shopping spree is asking myself: *What can I wear on a whim, and what truly expresses who I am?* Some classics are non\-negotiable: such as a white blouse with dress pants for interviews and networking, or a cozy sweater and jeans for the winter season\. But then, on other days, a really eccentric beanie is a must\.

## 5\. Style is affordable\.

We got you\! Thanks to our peer advisors, on Chapman Learning’s common blogs, we have created many resources that guide us toward building our own style affordably including [thrift stores](https://learningcommons.ubc.ca/dare-to-thrift-best-spots-to-shop-in-metro-vancouver/) and [free campus club resources\.](https://learningcommons.ubc.ca/i-tried-it-a-new-aesthetic-for-a-week/)

Like always, I hope this blog inspires you to embark on your own journey through styles and more at UBC\. Trust me when I say the world is now at your hem line\.

title: Navigating Long Distance Friendships/Relationships as an International Student
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/abdulrahman-lateef-DS7NUVn81iw-unsplash-1-890x960.jpg)

Leaving the life you’ve known, the people you grew up with, and your family to settle into another country is not an easy task\. Being an international student myself, I have gone through phases of extreme homesickness, missing friends back home and feeling left out of the hangouts/events in my hometown\. Watching through a screen is a blessing in today’s day and age, but it still doesn’t make the feeling of homesickness go away\.

Establishing a life in another country is time\-consuming, and sometimes you might get so caught up that you won’t realise when your friendships and relationships back home have started to drift a little\. I have been there as well, and now that I’m almost graduating, I hope my experiences help you navigate being in a long\-distance relationship with your loved ones\.  

Image by Abdulrahman Lateef on Unsplash

## Understanding the time\-difference

This might seem obvious, but I want to emphasise the importance of it\. Having a mutual understanding of the time zone between you and your loved ones is the first step in maintaining a bond\.

Image by By Francesca Albert on Unsplash 

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/francesca-albert-N-_lS9wbbho-unsplash-1-940x627.jpg)

Sometimes my friends would forget this and call me around 5 am, or I would forget and call them late at night\. It might take some time to get used to it\. A widget showing the time in your loved one’s city on your lockscreen might help in reminding you, as it helps me\. Eventually, though, planning your calls will become much easier\.

## Planning calls and hangouts

This might sound silly, but now that you’re not a car ride away and both you and your loved ones have opposing and busy schedules, planning a time for calls is probably the way to go\. I try to book some time off at least once every two weeks for catching up, where we would either just talk, study, watch a movie, or even play an online game together\! This has worked well in maintaining my relationships\. This way, my friends and I are always in the loop of what’s happening in our lives without disrupting our own schedules\. 

## Putting in the effort

Now that seeing your friends is not as easy, and you can’t tell if something is bothering them just by meeting them, putting in the effort to check\-in is always appreciated\. If I knew my friends or family might be going through a hard time, just sending a quick text or calling to remind them that I’m thinking of them goes a long way in keeping that bond intact\. We all get busy, especially in this phase of our lives, so being open\-minded and understanding of the changes that your relationships are bound to go through is extremely important\. 

Your relationships will not be the same as they used to be before you moved away, which is completely normal\. Growing together in this new phase of your lives, where you plan calls, text more often, and don’t communicate as much as you used to, is all part of the parcel of being an international student\. When you do go back home to visit, the feeling of nostalgia might linger to the time before you left, except with a hint of growth and exposure that will be worth it in the end\. 

## Every relationship is different

Lastly, I would like to point out that every relationship is different and everyone has their own unique way of continuing their bond even if they’re far apart\. These tips worked for me but might not work for you and that is alright\. Taking the time to talk it out with your loved one on how you want this to work might help you navigate the long\-distance and avoid the ever\-chasing feeling of growing distant\. Even if you do grow apart, which has happened to some of my relationships, being understanding of that will ironically also help maintain the bond\.

title: Ranking Local Fruits
content_markdown:
Did you know that UBC’s Point Grey campus is literally full of free food? The catch is that it’s all fruit\. But that’s hardly a downside\. After all, fruits are a great way to get your supply of antioxidants, vitamins, and fibers in\. They’re fairly portable, and they have numerous uses in cooking\.

During my time at UBC, I’ve had the privilege of trying several different local fruits\. Here, I’ll rank them from my least favourites to my favourites\. For the purpose of brevity, I’ll stick to lesser\-known fruits that are grown locally, either at a commercial level, or commonly enough in the wild that I can find them within walking distance of UBC’s Point Grey Campus \(mostly along Chancellor Boulevard\)\. With that said, here’s how I think Vancouver’s fruits stack up against each other:

## C\-Tier: Passable Produce

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/salal-berry-by-carlo-von-reyher-on-unsplash-940x627.jpg)

### **Salal berries**

#### *Gaultheria shallon*

I didn’t even realize these were edible the first time I encountered them\. They have a leathery, fuzzy skin, very little flesh or juice, and a ton of tiny seeds inside\. Interestingly, they’re apparently an appetite suppressant, and are said to improve when cooked, but for now I have to leave them in C\-tier\.

Image by [Carlo von Reyher](https://unsplash.com/photos/green-leaves-with-green-leaves-euIcR9443mk) on Unsplash

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/anne-nygard-OGSGDBvycwo-unsplash-940x627.jpg)

### **Salmon berries**

#### *Rubus spectabilis*

These gold or red berries are a lot like blackberries, but they have much larger seeds and seem to be available for a longer period of time throughout the year\. That said, they don’t get sweet like blackberries do, and I already find blackberries a little too seedy for my tastes, so I can’t place these higher than the top of C\-tier\.

Image by [Anne Nygård](https://unsplash.com/photos/a-bowl-of-fruit-OGSGDBvycwo) on Unsplash

## B\-Tier: Middle of the Bunch

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/amanda-hortiz-l1uVrvjZrsQ-unsplash.jpg)

### **Blackberries**

#### ***Rubus armeniacus***

These berries taste amazing, and you can pick them all along Chancellor Boulevard between early July and mid\-September for free\. That said, the wild ones are usually full of bugs\. It can take a lot of effort to get rid of them, and commercially available blackberries are usually expensive\. Regardless, blackberries are a solid BC staple and great to pick yourself during the summer in order to stock up for the winter\.

Image by [Amanda Hortiz](https://unsplash.com/photos/black-and-red-berries-in-tilt-shift-lens-l1uVrvjZrsQ) on Unsplash

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/photo-1566400628146-ae8f27849e90.avif)

### **Blueberries**

#### ***Vaccinium corymbosum***

All the benefits of blackberries, without the downsides\. Blueberries are easier to clean, much less seedy, and freeze better\. Overripe blueberries are especially gross, but that’s easy enough to avoid\.

Image by [Élisabeth Joly](https://unsplash.com/photos/selective-focus-photography-of-blue-berries-d7jhBvnZ9Pc) on Unsplash

## A\-Tier: A\-peel\-ing

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/huckleberries-732x960.png)

**Huckleberries**

#### ***Vaccinium parvifolium***

This is another one of those berries that you can pick around campus, but that aren’t really commercially sold\. Huckleberries are like blueberries, but they’re smaller, tarter, and go bright scarlet when ripe\. As far as the eating experience goes, they’re pretty much on par with blueberries in my opinion, but their availability near campus gives them a leg up\.

Image by Peer Assistant Ethaniel

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/burak-tonc-bbxwU3HtRkM-unsplash-720x960.jpg)

### **Cherries**

#### *Prunus avium*

Did you know that BC produces 95% of Canada’s cherries? There’s definitely no need for anyone else to try, because we do it right\. Cherries are delicious, raw or cooked, and provide myriad vitamins and antioxidants such as anthocyanids, Vitamin A, and quercetin\. They’re held out of S\-tier by their high cost, but are otherwise a quintessential BC experience that I refuse to rank anything lower than A\-tier\.

Image by [Burak Tonç](https://unsplash.com/photos/red-round-fruits-on-green-leaves-bbxwU3HtRkM) on Unsplash

## S\-Tier: The Berry Best

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/Thimbleberry_6000475585-940x666.jpg)

### **Thimbleberries**

#### ***Rubus parviflorus***

These are my absolute favourite foraging fruit\. They’re too fragile to survive commercial transport and so aren’t available in grocery stores, but you can find them all over campus, including on the west side of the Irving K\. Barber building\! They’re super sweet with a texture kind of like raspberries, though the seeds are much smaller and almost imperceptible when chewing\.

Image by [Leslie Seaton](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Thimbleberry_%286000475585%29.jpg) on Wikimedia

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/06/25043121385_a78fa2073e_c.jpg)

### **Golden plums**

#### *Prunus salicina* \(specifically the golden Japanese variety\)

A family friend of mine grows these in her backyard, and I remember trying them on vacation here when I was a kid\. When I moved to BC from Alberta later on in life, these plums were a distinct reason I was looking forward to living here\. They’re a complete mess to eat, but that’s more than made up for by the delicious contrast between the sweet flesh and delightfully tart skin\.

Image by [Forest and Kim Starr](https://www.flickr.com/photos/starr-environmental/25043121385/) on Flickr

---

…Hey, you made it to the end of my rankings\! I hope you learned something new about the amazing and bountiful fruits available on and around campus\. Let us know what your favourite fruits are in the comments below\!

title: Immune-Boosting Foods to Help You Stay Healthy During Classes
content_markdown:
There is nothing worse than waking up sick the week of midterms\. I have been there more times than I’d like to admit, sniffling through a lecture and surviving on cold medicine\. After one particularly rough flu season in second year, I started paying much more attention to what I was actually eating, and it made such a noticeable difference\. Here are seven foods I started adding into my routine that helped me get through the semester without completely falling apart\!

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/ben-ashby-TAqEFzBEKbY-unsplash-940x629.jpg)

## **Citrus Fruits**

They are going to be your body’s best friend when cold season hits\. I kept a bag of clementines on my desk during study sessions because they are cheap, easy to peel, and you can eat them without getting your keyboard sticky\. Squeezing lemon into hot water in the morning is also something I started doing almost by accident and it somehow became my favourite part of my morning\. If eating a whole orange feels like too much effort, just start there\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/sara-cervera-4caIPcmVDII-unsplash-940x625.jpg)

## **Yogurt**

This was an easy sell because who doesn’t like yogurt\! Studies show that your gut health has a lot to do with how often you get sick, and yogurt has probiotics that help with that\. I switched to plain Greek yogurt with honey and some fruit on top, and it became my go\-to breakfast on mornings when I had an 8am and no time to cook\. If plain yogurt sounds boring, adding a spoonful of peanut butter or some granola genuinely makes it feel like a real meal\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/ji-jiali-r8ySJfxvESQ-unsplash-940x528.jpg)

## **Garlic**

I know, I know, but hear me out\. I started throwing a clove or two into basically EVERYTHING I cooked\. Be it pasta sauce, stir fry or even roasted vegetables \(and after a while I stopped noticing it was even there\)\. The smell is honestly the biggest barrier, but cooking it down almost completely gets rid of it\. 

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/prchi-palwe-YUIMwavk7AQ-unsplash-940x627.jpg)

## **Turmeric**

This one is very easy to sneak into things\. I add a small pinch to rice, soups, and scrambled eggs, and I genuinely cannot taste it most of the time\. Turmeric golden milk before bed is also something I tried during finals and it became oddly calming, kind of like a warm hug in a mug\. Pro Tip: Add black pepper when you cook with it because it helps your body actually absorb it\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/kelly-sikkema-VQWiBp63eJQ-unsplash-940x627.jpg)

## **Ginger**

Ginger surprised me the most honestly\. I started making ginger tea on cold Vancouver mornings \(just a few slices boiled in water with honey\), and it became one of my favourite rituals\. It also settles your stomach if you are the type to stress\-eat your way through finals \(no judgment, same\)\. If you are feeling extra funky, ginger and turmeric shots are a thing at most grocery stores\. They taste intense for about three seconds and then you feel weirdly invincible, I promise\. 

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/aleksei-zhivilov-jim_U8LfJOw-unsplash-940x529.jpg)

## **Leafy Greens**

Okay, yes\. Obviously, leafy greens are on this list\. Nobody is surprised\. But the reason I am including them is because they are genuinely one of the easiest things to add without actually changing what you eat\. A handful of spinach in a smoothie? You cannot taste it\. Tossed into instant ramen? Takes two seconds\. Mixed into scrambled eggs? Barely noticeable\. You do not have to become a salad person, you just have to add a handful somewhere\!

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/maksim-shutov-pUa1On18Jno-unsplash-940x627.jpg)

## **Nuts and Seeds**

I started keeping a little container of mixed nuts in my bag after I realized I was getting to 3pm lectures, having eaten nothing since 9am\. Almonds, pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds, all genuinely good for keeping your immune system supported\. They also stopped me from spending four dollars on a granola bar from the vending machine every single day, which was a bonus\!

---

None of these are miracle cures, and I am definitely not a nutritionist\. But making small, consistent swaps, a handful of spinach here, a ginger tea there, has truly helped me feel more resilient during the parts of the semester when everyone around me was getting sick\. Even one or two of these added into your routine makes a real difference\!

What are your go\-to foods when you feel a cold coming on? Share them in the comments below\!

---

title: I Tried It: Using AI to Help Me Schedule/Organize My Life
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/solen-feyissa-hWSNT_Pp4x4-unsplash-940x627.jpg)

I have gone through all 4 years of my degree telling myself that THIS semester is when I am going to get organized and do everything I can to be the best version of myself\. Eat right, get 9 hours of sleep, study, workout, and have a social life\. Trying to figure this all out myself has proven to be difficult but I finally decided that I would use AI to help me optimize my life\. And here is how it went\.

## **The Prompt**

I started off with trying to figure out what it was that I wanted to allocate my time to effectively\. As someone who loves going to the gym, eating clean, and getting adequate amounts of sleep, I wanted to highlight the importance of having time for all of these things needed to be part of my regular schedule\. This helped me develop this prompt, which I plugged into ChatGPT so that it could create a schedule for me:

> *So, I am a 22 year old university student in my last year of university\. I value community, hard work, rest and having a few moments of self care in my day\. I like to eat whole foods which means dedicating some time in my week to meal prep and rest and sleep is very important to me\. I want to have at least 8 to 9 hours of sleep at night\. I value my time in the gym as well and I want to do a good job in school with my classes\. I want you to create a schedule for me based on my life so that I can achieve these goals\. I have class from Monday to Thursday at these times \(insert the times of your classes here\) and I work on these days at these times \(insert your work hours here\)\.*

I need time to study and do assignments\. I like to go to the gym in the morning and can be there for around 1 and a half to 2 hours\. Please make my schedule\.

## **My Experience**

When it finally gave me a schedule that I felt like I could work with, I tried it for a week\. I took note of the things I liked and didn’t find realistic for myself\. For example, it recommended that I do a debrief of my classes after every single class\. While this might be a good idea for some\. I didn’t find that it would be a great idea for me since I prefer dedicating large blocks of time towards my studying\.

## **Would I Recommend this to Someone Else?**

Now if anyone asks me if I think that this is something they should do, my answer is yes\! I found using AI to organize my life has given me a way to holistically account for the things that I value and ensure that I have enough time allocated to each thing\. I’ve found that using a planner or a calendar was just too rigid and did not allow for the flexibility that AI can account for\. For example, I can tell ChatGPT to adjust my schedule if I have an upcoming exam that I want more study time for, even telling it to break down what days I should start studying for each chapter\.

## **My Tips and Tricks**

For anyone wanting to use AI to schedule their lives, I would say:

-   Clearly outline any big goals or priorities that you have in your prompt\.
-   Don’t be afraid to tweak anything you don’t find realistic or feasible in the schedule it provides you\.
-   You can tweak the schedule again and again until it works for you\!

Let me know if you have any other tips on using AI to organize your life in the comments\!

title: I tried it! Rejection Therapy for a Week
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/image.png)

Image by Paul H Joseph

I’ve always been nervous about hearing the word no\. Whether it was asking a professor for an extension or trying to strike up a conversation with someone new, the idea of rejection has always made me freeze\. So, I decided to test myself with something called, drumroll please, Rejection Therapy\! The idea is to purposely put yourself in situations where people might say no, just to get used to it\. I tried it for one week, and here’s how it went\. 

**Day One:** I started small and asked the barista if I could get a student discount on my milkshake, even though I knew there wasn’t one\. She smiled and said no, but it wasn’t scary at all\. We even laughed about it and discussed how expensive Vancouver is\! Honestly, that little moment gave me more confidence to keep going

**Day Two:** It was raining \(not surprised, it’s Vancouver\), and I asked a stranger if I could borrow their umbrella\. I knew they’d say no, but that’s the point\. They looked surprised, shook their head, and walked away\. I FELT SO EMBARRASSED, but the worst thing that happened was a simple no, and that was it\. 

**Day Three:** After class, I asked my professor if I could get a sneak peek at next week’s quiz questions \(Yes, at this point, I was becoming a little more fearless each day\)\.

Obviously, they said no, but we ended up having a good conversation about study strategies\. I actually walked away with more help than I expected\. 

**Days Four and Five:** I went to three different places and politely asked for free fries\. Two of them laughed and said no \(very expected\)\. But one restaurant surprised me by bringing out complimentary nachos\. That little act of kindness made my whole day, and I was so grateful for it\. 

**Day Six and Seven:** To end the week, I asked a stranger if they would switch seats with me for a window spot on the bus\. I was prepared for a no, but they agreed right away\. We even exchanged a few pleasantries, and it felt like such a wholesome moment\. It showed me that sometimes you brace yourself for rejection, but people surprise you with kindness\. 

After seven days, I stopped seeing rejection as a big, scary thing\. Most of the time, it was just a short moment and then life went on\. Sometimes it even led to better conversations\. Rejection therapy doesn’t make you fearless, but it makes you realise rejection doesn’t define you\. Once I started thinking “rejection is just redirection,” life became easier\. 

So why not seize the day? Ask your crush out on a date, ask your professor for advice on something that scares you, or ask your roommate to join you on a spontaneous adventure\. What’s the worst that can happen? They say no\. But it’s better than not knowing which no might have turned into a yes\. 

You are always one question away from changing your life\. Let us know in the comments what you think about trying rejection therapy\!

title: Following Someone Else’s Path vs. Following Your Own
content_markdown:
Have you ever felt like you’re walking a path that doesn’t quite feel like yours?

At university, it can get incredibly easy to believe there is a “right” or a “perfect” way to do things\. Surrounded by high achievers, I always felt like everyone else had it figured out and I started making choices based on what looked good on a resume or what I thought would make others proud\.

But even when my life made perfect sense on paper, something felt off to me\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/jens-lelie-u0vgcIOQG08-unsplash-940x629.jpg)

*Photo by [Jens Lelie](https://unsplash.com/@madebyjens?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/@madebyjens?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)*

## The Comparison Trap

My biggest hurdle was comparison\. I looked up to people I admired, and I unconsciously tried to follow their exact paths\. Somewhere along the way, I lost track of what I actually wanted and I didn’t realize I had started to live a life driven by someone else’s goals\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/priscilla-du-preez-K8XYGbw4Ahg-unsplash-940x627.jpg)

Photo by [Priscilla Du Preez](https://unsplash.com/@priscilladupreez?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/woman-in-black-long-sleeve-shirt-holding-black-ceramic-mug-K8XYGbw4Ahg?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

## Shifting My Perspective

What changed things for me was taking a step back\. I decided to speak with a university counsellor and career advisor, and answering just a few simple questions made me pause and that’s when I realized the path I was on wasn’t mine\.

Of course I still don’t have everything figured out, but I’ve started being more intentional\. If you’re feeling “stuck” in a plan that doesn’t seem like *you*, here is what helped me:

-   **Ask “Why?”:** I started questioning if I was making decisions for myself or for the resume\.
-   **Follow Your Interest:** I started to pay closer attention to the topics that actually kept me engaged in lectures\.
-   **Embrace Newness:** I tried small things like taking electives and joining clubs that felt right, even if they didn’t fit my five\-year plan\.
-   **Talk It Out:** I stopped keeping my doubts in my head and started talking to my mentors\.

## Trusting the process

It’s easy to feel like you need a perfectly figured out life in university, but that isn’t realistic\. Figuring things out *is* the process and the sooner we realise, the more we can use our resources to the fullest extent\. Deciding to follow my own path didn’t happen overnight, it started with small changes and a lot of honesty\. It still feels uncertain sometimes, but it feels a lot more *real* than following a path that was never mine\.

title: I Tried It! Keeping a Dream Journal for a Week
content_markdown:
I have always had the weirdest dreams\. Like one time, I was running late for class on a flying toaster, and this other time I was trapped in an orange juice box in the fridge, tormenting the vegetables\. I never thought much of my dreams, and honestly, I forget most of the story within thirty minutes of waking up\.

Recently,I thought to myself, “Wait, what if my brain is actually hiding something smart?” Basically, I convinced myself my dreams could make me a millionaire\. So I decided to try keeping a dream journal for a week to see if I’d unlock my subconscious… or just find out I dream about cereal way more than the average person\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/johannes-plenio-DKix6Un55mw-unsplash-1-940x610.jpg)

Image by [Johannes Plenio](https://unsplash.com/photos/black-sailing-boat-digital-wallpaper-DKix6Un55mw) on Unsplash

I decided to record my dreams in a cute little notebook, but you can use literally anything: notes app, sticky notes, voice memos, whatever works\. The real struggle was actually remembering the dream before it vanished\. I swear I’d wake up and five seconds later, I’d be like, “Wait… why was there a horse in my kitchen?” On Day 1, I just wrote one messy line: “something about the Great Wall of China??” No context\. But even that tiny line made me realise something\. I forget everything WAY faster than I think I do\. That was my first mini\-lesson\. Remembering things isn’t just about memory; it’s about slowing down long enough to notice them\.

By the third or fourth morning, I started spotting actual patterns\. Apparently, my brain loves movement, running, chasing, being chased, and climbing stairs for no reason\. I also kept dreaming about food \(like… a concerning amount\)\. But what surprised me was how these themes reflected what was happening in my real life\. On days I was stressed, the dreams were chaotic\. On days I went to bed happy or tired, the dreams were softer\. I’m not saying dreams reveal your destiny or anything, but they definitely mirror the mood you’ve been carrying around\.

Doing this little ritual every morning felt strange at first\. I’d sit there half\-asleep, struggling to write\. But after a few days, it became grounding in a way I didn’t expect\. It forced me to start my day slowly instead of immediately reaching for my phone\. It was weirdly calming to write something down before getting on with my day, and it made me realize I never give myself a moment to reflect, even just on silly things like dreams\. It might sound small, but it made my mornings feel… gentler\. A little more human\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/07/35392664584_dd717084d1_k-940x627.jpg)

Image from UBC Media Relations

Keeping a dream journal didn’t turn me into some dream expert, but it made me appreciate how busy the brain is even when we’re “resting”\. Fun fact: we dream for about two hours every night, even if we remember none of it\. So your brain is literally storytelling while you sleep\. Recording my dreams helped me see tiny emotional patterns I wouldn’t notice otherwise, how stress shows up, how little fears sneak in, how my mind processes things I didn’t even realize I was holding onto\.

If you’re someone who likes understanding yourself better, or you’re curious about why your brain does what it does, you might genuinely enjoy dream journaling\. It’s not just “writing weird stuff”, it’s like checking in with a part of your mind that never gets to speak\. And if you’re not into analysing anything, it’s still a fun way to get a free laugh every morning\.

Feel free to share what you’ve been dreaming about in the comments below\!

title: When Everything Lives On A Screen: How I’m Rethinking Screen Time
content_markdown:
Somewhere between online lectures, digital planners, group chats, and endless tabs open on my laptop, I recently realized how much of my day was spent staring at a screen\. Not just for school, but for *everything*\. Studying, planning, procrastinating, unwinding; it all happened on different glowing rectangles\.

I wasn’t necessarily *unproductive*\. I was getting things done\. But I constantly felt behind, overstimulated, and weirdly exhausted; even on days when I hadn’t physically done much at all\. That’s when I started noticing how closely my screen time and time management were tied together\. Spending more time on screens made it harder to focus, plan my time, and fully commit to one task at a time\.

With the start of a new year, I found myself thinking a lot about the kinds of goals I wanted to set, not the dramatic, all\-or\-nothing kind, but ones that felt realistic and sustainable\. Being more intentional with my screen time and how I manage my time overall became one of those goals\. I wasn’t aiming to cut screens out completely; I just wanted to be more aware of how often I was reaching for them and whether they were actually supporting what I needed at that moment\.

## Productivity vs\. Presence

One of the biggest shifts for me was noticing how often I equated *being busy* with *being* *productive*\. I’d spend hours switching between tabs and tasks, convincing myself I was making progress, even when my focus was scattered\.

Screen time made it harder to feel present in what I was doing\. I wasn’t fully resting when I took breaks, because those breaks usually involved more scrolling\. And I wasn’t fully focused when I worked, because distractions were always one click away\.

Over time, this constant half\-focus made managing my time feel harder than it needed to be\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/08/annie-spratt-QckxruozjRg-unsplash-940x627.jpg)

[*Image by Annie Spratt from Unsplash*](https://unsplash.com/photos/group-of-people-using-laptop-computer-QckxruozjRg)

## Small Changes That Actually Helped

I didn’t overhaul my entire routine overnight\. Instead, I focused on small, realistic changes that felt sustainable\.

-   **Being intentional with how I opened my laptop:** I started sitting down with one clear task in mind instead of opening everything at once and hoping for the best\.
-   **Working in shorter blocks with non\-screen breaks:** Stepping away, even for five minutes, helped reset my focus far better than scrolling ever did\.
-   **Not starting my mornings with my phone:** This became one of my goals for the year\. As tempting as it is to scroll after hitting snooze for the millionth time, skipping that habit actually made waking up feel easier and helped me feel more grounded\.
-   **Checking in with why I was reaching for a screen:** Sometimes scrolling was a genuine way to unwind and at other times, it was just procrastination dressed up as “a break\.”
-   **Create one screen\-free buffer in the day:** I picked just one moment— either the first hour of my morning or an hour before bed — to stay off my phone\. Keeping it small helped me ease into the habit without feeling overwhelmed\.
-   **Separate “work screens” from “rest screens”:** I tried to keep my laptop strictly for schoolwork and my phone for personal use, so my work time felt more contained\. When I needed a break, I avoided opening new apps on my laptop and instead gave myself a proper pause\.
-   **End work sessions with a clear stopping point:** Instead of working until I felt exhausted, I started stopping after finishing one specific task\. This gave my work sessions a clearer end, rather than letting them stretch on without structure\.

## Letting Go of “Perfect” Time Management

What I’ve learned is that time management isn’t about squeezing as much productivity as possible into a day\. It’s about creating enough structure to support your energy, focus, and well\-being\.

Screens aren’t going anywhere, especially in student life, but learning how to work *with* them instead of letting them dictate your time has helped me feel more in control of my days\.

I’m still figuring it out\. Some weeks are better than others\. But being more mindful of my screen habits has made managing my time feel less overwhelming and more intentional\.

I’m still learning what works best for me, so if you have any tips or habits that help you limit screen time, feel free to share them in the comments\.

title: I Tried It! Budgeting With Cash Envelopes (aka “Cash Stuffing”)
content_markdown:
[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/08/image-940x627.jpeg)

Photo by [Frugal Flyer](https://unsplash.com/@frugalflyer?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/calendar-VbdUnqoe5UU?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

Scrolling through TikTok a few months ago, I kept seeing people “cash stuffing” portions of their paychecks and spare bills into cute envelopes\. At first, I thought, *this is way too extra for me*\. But then I remembered how easily I swipe my card, so I figured why not give it a shot? Worst case, I’d end up with a stack of envelopes and a funny story\. Best case, I’d finally get a handle on my random spending\. 

## What is the Envelope System?

The envelope system is pretty simple: you divide up your money \(usually from each payday or month\) into different categories: groceries, dining out, gas, entertainment, etc\. Each category gets its own envelope\. Once the cash in an envelope is gone, that’s it for spending in that category until the next refill\. The idea is: if the money’s not available physically, you’re less likely to overspend\. 

You can use physical envelopes \(actual cash\), or a digital version \(apps or spreadsheets that mimic the envelopes\)\. [Capital One](https://www.capitalone.com/learn-grow/money-management/envelope-budget-system/) describes both approaches and emphasizes that this system is especially useful for *variable expenses*, the ones that tend to fluctuate every month\.

## How I Set It Up?

### Here’s what I did:

1.  **Chose my categories**: I looked through my bank statements from the past few months to figure out where my money was going\. I picked 5\-6 variable spending categories: groceries, eating out, entertainment, personal care, and “miscellaneous”\. 
2.  **Assigned amounts:** Based on historical spending, I decided how much cash I’d allot to each envelope per month \(I left a little wiggle room, just in case\)\.
3.  **Got the cash:** On payday, I withdrew the total envelope money I needed\. Then I divided it up into the designated envelopes\. 
4.  **Tracked as I spent:** I marked down how much I took from each envelope, and kept a running total so I could see what I had left\. I kept the amounts written on the envelopes themselves so I could see my balance right away \(but a small tracker sheet or phone note works too\)\. 
5.  **No refill until reset:** Once an envelope was empty, I tried to avoid dipping into others \(though I did once or twice\)\.  
    

## What was good?

-   **More Awareness of Spending:** Seeing cash physically leave an envelope made me more conscious of spending\. I hesitated more often before buying non\-essentials\. There was something grounding about it; I’d pause and ask myself, “Do I really want this, or is it just a momentary craving?” Sometimes I’d even put the item back and feel oddly proud of that small act of restraint\. Writing down the remaining amount on the envelope after each purchase also made me realize how quickly small expenses add up, it turns numbers on a screen into something tangible\.
-   **Motivation to Save Leftovers:** If I had cash left over, I felt proud keeping it, or using it for something I’ve been wanting, like a nice dinner, or putting it toward savings\.

[Image](https://lc2023.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2026/08/image-1-940x539.jpeg)

## Digital vs Physical : What I Learned

I tried both ways:

-   Physical cash envelopes feel more tangible\. The act of handing over cash hits differently than swiping a card\. 
-   But digital envelopes \(via a spreadsheet\) are more convenient for me, especially for online purchases, bills, or simply when I don’t have cash on me\. 

## Verdict : Will I Keep Doing It?

Yes, but with a few tweaks\. I think a hybrid method may be the sweet spot for me: physical for groceries, maybe digital for categories I usually buy things online for or that require card payments\. 

The envelope system taught me a lot about where my money was going and helped me pause before impulse buys\. Even though “ideal” didn’t always happen, I found it helpful enough that I’m sticking with a version that works for me\. 

## Tips If You Want to Try It

-   Start small: pick a couple of categories first\. Don’t try to envelope everything\.
-   Use your past spending data to set amounts \(look at the last 2–3 months\)\.
-   Track rigorously \(or try to\): writing down or logging every expense helps more than you think\.
-   Allow margin for surprises: occasional buffer money helps reduce stress\.
-   Adjust as you go: if something isn’t working, change it\. Budgets aren’t one\-size\-fits\-all\.

## About the Zine

As the summer session comes to an end, we are proud to release our fifth edition of the Chapman Learning Commons Zine, a collection of art pieces, written works, and creative design, created and curated by our Student Staff\.

The end of summer brings a new cohort of fresh students to UBC, ready to experience this university that is so special to us for the first\-time\. Being a first\-year is not easy, whether it’s adjusting to university\-level classes, living away from home for the first time, or even just making friends\. That’s why we decided to make our First Year Survival Guide\.

Even if you are not a first\-year and are returning to UBC after the summer, this zine is sure to share some new information with you or even tell you a trick about campus you may not have known\. After all, UBC is full of surprises\!

We wish all UBC students the best of luck, as we all embark on a new academic year together\. It is not easy, but the people, this campus, and the community that we have at UBC makes even the lowest of lows feel doable\. So, as the weather starts to become slightly cooler and the days shorter and shorter with every passing night, it’s important to welcome the new academic year that is upon us with open arms, however hard it may feel in the moment\. To the first\-years, we know this can be a daunting time, but we hope you find what you are looking for in this zine\. And to everybody else, we hope you not only “survive” but thrive this year\.

Have a great year,

*Your Summer 2026 CLC Assistants*

## UBC Imagine Day Information

*Written by Dana*

### For First\-Year and New to UBC Students

There are no classes for most students on Imagine Day UBC\! Students can follow their personalized schedule that was sent to them in late\-August\.

Faculties have their own orientation events\! Students should keep an eye out for emails from their faculty before Imagine Day to get them oriented through UBC platforms and get notified about future events\.

Indigenous students can find more orientation resources and spaces from the First Nations House of Learning and šxʷta:təχʷəm\!

### Imagine Day Checklist

-   Finding my Orientation Group information \(from email\)
-   Getting my UBC Student Card
-   Signing up for my U\-Pass
-   Wearing my Faculty colour

-   [Imagine Day Accessibility FAQ](https://orientations.students.ubc.ca/accessibility-faq)

*List by Selena*

🐚 Climb the Wreck Beach stairs

🏈 Go to a UBC Thunderbirds football game

🚣 Day of the Longboat

🧱 Storm the Wall

🏞️ Walk a trail at Pacific Spirit Park
